Probir Neogi, Advocate ------ For the Appellant in the first appeal and respondent 1 in the cross objection. 
Ali Imam Khaled Rahim ------ For Respondent 1 in the first appeal and objector in the cross objection.
parties:
Bohumukhi Samabaya Samity Ltd ------ Appellant
Vs.
Md Nazrul Islam and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khasruzzaman J: The above noted first appeal, at the instance of the plaintiff Mirpur section No. 6 Bohumukhi Samabai Samity Ltd, was preferred against the judgment and decree dated 6-6-2012 (decree signed on 14-6-2012) passed by the Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit 14 of 2012 analogously heard and disposed of with Title Suit No. 13 of 2012 (Md Nazrul Islam vs Mirpur Section No. 6 Bohumukhi Samabai Samity Ltd.) decreeing the suit (Title Suit No. 14 of 2012) by awarding Taka 85,45,000 in favour of the plaintiff-samity. 

 2. The plaintiff-samity instituted Title Suit No. 46 of 2005 on 9-2-2005 for specific performance of contract impleading the vendor Md Nazrul Islam as principal defendant. Subsequently, the suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 14 of 2012 on transfer to the Additional Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka. 

 3. Prior to filing of the suit, the vendor Md Nazrul Islam had instituted Title Suit No. 383 of 2004 impleading the samity as defendant for a declaration that the contract for sale in question was void and not binding upon him. The suit was also renumbered as Title Suit No. 13 of 2012 on transfer to the same Court. 

 4. The case of the plaintiff-samity is same as that of defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 13 of 2012 and the case of the plaintiff-vendor in Title Suit No. 13 of 2012 is same as that of defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012. Both the suits were heard analogously and were disposed of by a single judgment dated 6-6-2012. 

 5. The case of the plaintiff-samity, in short, is that the suit land belonged to the Government in the Settlement and Housing Department under the Ministry of Works, which leased out the same to one Gazanfar Ali for 99 years and handed over the possession thereof. The said Gazanfar Ali made construction on the suit land according to a plan approved by RAJUK. The vendor Md. Nazrul Islam purchased the suit property from the said Gazanfar Ali by a registered sale deed being No. 4278 dated 15-10-1992, and constructed a multi-storied building thereon as per a revised plan duly approved by RAJUK. The General Secretary of the plaintiff-samity Mr Md Abdul Manna, and a member Md. Sobhan purchased the possession of shop Nos. 1 and 2 respectively situated on the ground floor. The vendor, Md Nazrul Islam, executed an instrument of transfer of possession on 22-2-1993 to that effect. Subsequently, he obtained loan of Taka 25,00,000 lakh from Janata Bank, Mirpur Branch (defendant No. 4 in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012) on 19-11-1997 and mortgaged the suit property to the bank as security suppressing the fact of selling possession of two shops. In order to complete the construction of the six-storied building, he also took loan from the plaintiff-samity, and sold possession of the first and second floors to seventy shareholders of its Commercial Project No. 1 for consideration of Taka 7,00,000 (seven lakh) on 3-3-1998 and Taka 7,00,000 (seven lakh) on 23-5-1998 respectively. The .vendor Md Nazrul Islam entered into an agreement for sale of the third floor to one Md Manir-ul-Islam and Md Abdul Quaiyum on 18-6-1998 and received Taka 7,50,000 lakh (seven lakh fifty thousand) from them, who subsequently transferred the possession of the 3rd (third) floor to the samity on receiving Taka 7,50,000 lakh (seven lakh fifty thousand). Then he took Taka 5,50,000 lakh (five lakh fifty thousand) on 4-1-1999 from one Md Mobin Khan, a member of the samity for transfer of possession of the fourth floor and took Taka 4,25,000 (four lakh twenty-five thousand) from the samity for transfer of the possession of the fifth floor, which was still under construction. In this way the vendor received Taka 36,01,000 in total from the samity and some of its members for transfer of possession of all the floors of the building. 

 6. Thereafter, he entered into an agreement for sale of the suit property to the samity at a consideration of, Taka- 85,50,000 (eighty-five lakh fifty thousand) and handed over its possession to the samity. It was stipulated that the vendor, after obtaining sale permission from Housing and Settlement. Directorate, would execute and register, a proper sale deed, but took no, measures to that effect. He also shifted his liability to Janata Bank upon the samity, and accordingly a tri-partite negotiation between the bank, vendor and samity was held on 28-2-1999 at Janata Bank, Mirpur-10 Branch and an adjustment of the liability regarding the vendor's bank loan was undertaken by the samity in writing. The samity accordingly paid the entire loan of the vendor amounting to Taka 24,52,556 (twenty-four lakh fifty-two thousand five hundred fifty-six) in total to the bank. The vendor himself also received Taka 24,30,000 (twenty-four lakh thirty thousand) in cash and Taka 25,00,000 (twenty-five lakh) by way of refund of bank loan and additional amounts of Taka 36,01,000 from time to time from the samity and acknowledged receipts thereof. Thereafter, he received some more amount from the samity. The total amounts taken by him thus Comes to Taka 85,45,000 (eighty-five lakh forty-five thousand). As he refused to execute the sale deed, the samity was constrained to tile: Title Suit No. 14 of 2012. 

 7. The vendor Md Nazrul Islam contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to the Housing and Settlement Directorate under the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, who leased it out to one Gazanfar Ali, from whom he had purchased the suit property by a registered sale deed dated 15-10-1992 and constructed a multi-storied building thereon as per revised construction plan duly approved by RAJUK. 

 9. The samity has been misappropriating lakhs of money by continuing its forceful and illegal possession over the property, which compelled him to institute Title Suit No. 13 of 2012 for a declaration that the agreement for sale is not binding on him. The samity instituted the present Title Suit No. 14 of 2012 for specific performance of contract just to frustrate his suit. Thus he prayed for dismissal of Title Suit No. 14 of 2012. 

 10. The proforma defendant Nos. 2 and 3 (in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012), the Chairman, National Housing Authority and its Director, Land and Estate Management in their joint written statement, amongst others, stated that the suit land was allotted to one Gazanfar Ali by a letter of allotment dated 18-7-1981 and the possession thereof was handed over to him on 19-10-1981. Thereafter, a lease deed being No. 1361 dated 13-3-1989 was executed and registered in his favour after payment of the total consideration money got a plan approved by RAJUK for construction of a seven-storied building thereon. He, however, sold out the suit land by a registered sale deed being No. 4278 dated 15-10-1992 to Md Nazrul Islam (the principal defendant in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012). He got the record mutated in his name by filing an application on 12-7-1992 and obtained a non-encumbrance certificate on 24-6-1997. They had no knowledge of the agreement for sale as no application seeking sale permission was filed to them. If anyone wants to sell a plot/house/flat under their control, he is to pay a particular amount of fees on deposition of which, the authority gives him the sale permission. There is no provision to sell a plot/house/flat without any sale permission. 

 12. To prove their respective claims Md Abdul Mannan, General Secretary of the plaintiff-samity in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012 and Md Nazrul Islam, plaintiff in Title Suit No. 13 of 2012 were examined as witnesses. 

 13. Md Abdul Mannan PW 1 in his deposition supported the plaint case described in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012 and produced some documents which were marked as exhibit Nos. 1, 2- 2(Gha), 3, 4-4 (Ka), 5, 6, 7-7 (Gha), 8-8(Ga), 9-9 (Ha), 10, 11,12. 

 14. On the other hand Md. Nazrul Islam deposed in Title Suit No.14 of 2012 as DW 1. In his evidence he stated that he had executed the agreements for sale after receiving the earnest money and handed over possession of the scheduled property in favour of the plaintiff-samity and also executed a nadabipatro in support of the proposed sale. His wife, son and daughter were the witnesses to the said nadabipatro. His signatures on different dates acknowledging receipt of the money were correct thus admitted execution of the two sale agreements and passing of consideration money as well as delivery of possession in favour of the plaintiff-samity. 

 15. After conclusion of trial, the learned Joint District Judge found the contract to be genuinely made on passing of consideration money from the purchaser to the vendor, and accordingly dismissed Title Suit No 13 of 2012, and also refused to enforce the contract as prayed, in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012 by thee impugned judgment and decree. The learned Judge, however, passed a decree for payment of Taka 85,45,000 in favour of, the plaintiff-samity holding that the bank is still the lawful owner of the suit land as the same was not redeemed. In such a position no one is legally entitled to transfer the mortgaged property without redemption. 

 16. Md Nazrul Islam as cross objector filed the aforesaid cross objection against the judgment and decree dated 6-6-2012 (Decree signed on 14-6-2012) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka decreeing the Title Suit No. 14 of 2012, so far it relates to the defendant-respondent having received summons of FA No. 267 of 2012 by the respondent No. 1 which was heard analogously with this instant appeal and disposed of by this judgment. 

 17. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant in First Appeal No. 267 of 2012 has submitted that in a suit for specific performance of contract the essential legal requirements that need to be proved are that whether the contract was genuine, consideration money was passed and delivery of possession was given in pursuance thereof, where part performance is pleaded. In view of this established principle of law and having regard to the trial Court's own findings, it ought to have decreed the suit for specific performance of contract instead of passing a decree for payment of money. In support of his contention he cited the case of Minhazuddin Talukder vs Abdul Jalil Howlader, 3 MLR (AD) 58. 

 18. Learned Advocate further submitted that where the above mentioned legal requirements are fulfilled, the Court is competent to pass a decree of specific performance and that is why the National Housing Authority and Janata Bank have been impleaded as proforma defendants in the present suit. It is also settled that a suit cannot be defeated on the ground that the vendor did not obtain sale permission from defendant Nos. 2-3 and for want of redemption. If the suit is decreed for specific performance, the vendor will be directed to execute and register the sale deed after obtaining sale permission within the time as specified in the decree failing which the plaintiff will be entitled to get the sale deed executed and registered through Court, and in that case the defendant No. 4 will also be bound to accord necessary permission and execute a redemption deed in obedience to the decree of civil court. In support of his contention he cited the cases of Motilal vs Nanhelal, 35 CWN 93, and Gokul vs Haji, 42 CWN 97. 

 25. Mr Rahim referred to section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and submits that the law does not allow a lessee to transfer his interest unless he is authorized to do so by the lessor. In the present case no sale permission was given by the Housing Authority and the transfer without written permission was also restricted by the lease deed and the lessor by filing written statement expressing his unwillingness. The sale permission being a condition precedent to transfer the land, the suit is not maintainable, since admittedly no permission has been given. The Court cannot direct the Housing Authority to grant permission because the authority is not a party to the contract. An agreement that opposes the law is void as per the provision of section 23 of the Contract Act. In paragraph 7 of the plaint, the plaintiff specifically stated that the vendor entered into an agreement for selling the property at a consideration of Taka 85,45,000. While in paragraph 9 it is specifically stated that the agreement was executed on 14-3-2000. Exhibit 4 is another agreement for sale which was signed only by the vendor. A single party in an agreement cannot make a contract. Therefore, this is not enforceable. Moreover, in the said agreement dated 14-3-2000 (exhibit 4) it is specifically stated 

 In paragraph 9 of the plaint in Title Suit No. 14 of 2012, the plaintiff-samity specifically stated that the vendor took Taka 24,30,000.00 from the samity, Taka 25,00,000 towards repayment bank loan and Taka 36,01,000 for transferring possession of the shop/floor to the samity. In this way he took Taka 85,31,000 in total and thereafter, received some more money which comes to Taka 85,45,000 in total and executed the sale agreement. Since specific statement in the contract is admittedly not correct, it is not safe to rely upon other contents of the same. The vendor signed each and every document produced by the samity, although those documents contains many errors and uncertainties those were rectified subsequently after the signature was taken. This again shows that the vendor was not in a position to bargain rather had to give his consent unwillingly. 

 26. Mr Rahim lastly submitted that since the samity did not come before the Court with clean hand for equitable relief, cannot get a decree for specific performance and furthermore as per section 65 of the Contract Act the samity may be entitled to the money which was actually spent and the vendor is entitled to get a decree for recovery of possession. 

 27. PW 1 Md Abdul Mannan in his examination-in-chief stated that he was the General Secretary of the samity which was registered under the Co-operative Society Act and had 70 share-holders. On behalf of the samity he entered into the agreement in the capacity of its General Secretary The suit property originally belonged to National Housing Authority which gave settlement of the same to one Gazanfar Ali on 20-8-1989, who sold it to the defendant Nazrul Islam. The said Nazrul Islam after obtaining approval of a revised plan initially constructed two shops thereon and sold one to him at a consideration of Taka 2,25,500 on 10-2-1993 and another to Sobhan at a consideration of Taka 2,50,000 on 22-2-1993. He took loan of Taka 25,00,000 lakh on 19-11-1997 from Janata Bank by mortgaging the suit property for, construction of a six-storied building. On completion of part construction sold the first floor to Moshiur at a consideration of Taka 7,00,000 on 3-3-1998, second floor to the samity at a consideration of Taka 7,00,000 third floor to Monirul and Quaiyum at a consideration of Taka 7,50,000 and fourth floor to Md Jalil Kha at a consideration of Taka 5,50,000. He also took Taka 4,25,000 to sell the fifth floor and basement and in this way received Taka 36,01,000 in total through vouchers. He received the money by endorsement on back page of the deed. As he failed to construct the building as per plan, he proposed the samity to purchase the entire building with the land and Taka 85,50,000 was fixed as the consideration money. The agreement was signed by the President and Secretary of the samity. It was agreed that after repaying the bank's loan of Taka 25,00,000 and after obtaining the sale permission from the. Housing Authority, the deed of conveyance would be executed and registered on receipt of the rest of the consideration money. Although the plaintiff paid the money according to the agreement, the defendant failed to execute the deed of conveyance. There was a tripartite meeting held at Janata Bank and it was agreed that the loan of Taka 25,00,000 would be paid by the samity and accordingly the money was paid. The defendant Nazrul Islam received the consideration money through debit and credit vouchers and on making endorsement on the back page of the agreement he received Taka 24,30,000. He further received Taka 36,01,000 from the possession holders of two shops on the ground floor, 1st, 2nd and 4th floors and handed over possession thereof to the lease holders. In this way the defendant received Taka 85,45,000 in total. He handed over the possession of the building and executed a 'na-dabinama' wherein his wife, son and daughter put their signatures as attesting witnesses. After payment of the full consideration money, the samity requested him to execute the sale deed on obtaining sale permission from the Housing Authority and to redeem the mortgaged property from the bank, but he failed to do so, for which the plaintiff-samity through its lawyer sent a legal notice on- 12-1-2005. 

 29. In cross-examination he stated that he was the General Secretary of the samity and was still holding that position. The total share holders of the samity were 70 in number. The registration number of the samity was 83/95. He executed the sale agreement on behalf of the samity. They had taken resolution to that effect. He could not remember, the date of the resolution but stated that the date was mentioned in the plaint. The another sale agreement was executed on 14-3-2000 but was not registered. There was also a na-dabinama. Total consideration money was fixed at Taka 85,50,000 on 14-3-2000. They paid Taka 85,45,000 on different dates, but he could not remember that whether this statement was written in the sale agreement. The rest of the amount was Taka 5,000. The defendant received the aforesaid money in cash and through cheques by making endorsement on the back page of the deed. He could not remember how many cheques and what amount was paid through the cheques to the defendant No. 1. He stated these facts in his plaint and also in his examination-in-chief. Defendant No. 1 owed Taka 49,53,000 (forty-nine lakh fifty-three thousand). He knew that the land belonged to the Housing Estate and he executed the sale agreement before obtaining sale permission. There is a six-storied building including basement on the suit land and a plan was approved to construct the building in the name of the defendant Nazrul Islam. The possession of the building was handed over to them on 14-3-2000. They leased out part of the building to different tenants and we residing in the remaining part. He denied that they earned Taka 3,00,000 as rent from the building or that they misappropriated the rent received from the tenants He also denied that the bank loan of the defendant was paid from the rent of the building and that they created an unregistered sale agreement fraudulently, or that the signature of the defendant was taken in the agreement fraudulently. 

 33. It is thus evident that the vendor did not deny the execution of the two agreements but he only disputes the amount of money paid to him. So, we are of the view that the contract is a genuine one and the recital of the agreement and his signatures on the back page of the agreement showing payment also prove that the consideration money was passed. It reveals from exhibit 7-8 series that possession was handed over to the members of the plaintiff-samity, which the DW 1 also admitted. We, therefore, find no illegality with the findings of the trial Court. The trial Court ought to have decreed the suit for specific performance of contract. This view finds support from the cited case of Minhazuddin Talukder vs Abdul Jalil Howlader, 3 MLR (AD) 58. 

 34. Admittedly, the loan taken by of the vendor from Janata Bank was paid by the plaintiff-samity. It also paid Taka 24,30,000 (admitted by the vendor though the disputed certain amount) and accordingly the vendor handed over possession of the property to the samity, who now is in possession of the suit property. 

 35. On perusal of the record we have also found that the vendor entered into two agreements with the plaintiff-samity for sale of the suit property and also executed and signed a na-dabinama in favour of the samity. The vendor admitted the execution of the agreement but disputed receipt of certain amount of money and entries on the agreement. So the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent that the vendor was not in a position either to check the correctness of the entries or to go through the contents of the document and since he had no equal bargaining power, his consent was not free, and it rather was obtained by some other manner indicating fraud, is not acceptable. 

 36. It is true that section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 does not allow a lessee to transfer his interest unless he is authorized to do so by the lessor. In the present case no sale permission is given by the Housing Authority and the transfer without written permission is also restricted expressly by the lease deed. The sale permission was a condition precedent to transfer the land and admittedly no permission has been given. But mere signing of the contract was not sale, it was an agreement for sale and the permission is yet to be accorded. According to the cases of Motilal vs Nanhelal, 35 CWN 93, and Gokul vs Haji, 42 CWN 97 cited by the plaintiff-appellant, the civil Court is competent to pass a decree for specific performance and to direct the vendor to execute and register the sale deed after obtaining sale permission from the authority concerned and redemption of the mortgage from the bank within a specified time failing which the plaintiff will be entitled to get the sale deed executed and registered through Court, and in that event the proforma defendants will be bound to accord necessary permission for sale and to redeem the mortgage property in compliance with the decree. We are in agreement with the above cited decisions. 

 39. We find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant and as such the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree as prayed for. 

 40. In the result, the First Appeal No. 267 of 2012 is allowed and the Title Suit No.14 of 2012 is decreed. The Cross Objection No. 2 of 2013 is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

 41. The defendant-respondent vendor Md Nazrul Islam is directed to execute and register a sale deed in respect of the scheduled property in favour of the plaintiff-samity on receipt of Taka 20,00,000 (twenty lakh) as solatium after obtaining sale permission from the National Housing Authority and redemption of the mortgaged property from the bank within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of the judgment, failing which the plaintiff-samity is entitled to get the sale deed registered through Court.
